correctness.rationale: Plancherel gives the asserted operator norm at positive integer order, and y=sin²(theta/2) maps the whole circle onto [0,1] with difference amplitude 2 sqrt(y). Normalized real even symbols of degree at most two are exactly q(y)=1-a*y+b*y². For r=kappa/2>0 and h>(r+2)/r, the ratio ((r+2)h-r)/(rh-r-2) decreases strictly from infinity to (r+2)/r, whereas h^(r+1) increases unboundedly. This proves the first root prescription including uniqueness. Q(z)=1-Az+Bz² has Q(h)<0, Q'(h)>0 and B>0. Beyond its zero on (h,infinity), z^r Q(z) increases strictly from zero to infinity, so the second positive-level equation has exactly one solution. Differentiating the candidate weighted polynomial gives (r/h)y^(r-1)(zy-1)(zy-h), so the interior extrema are 1/z and h/z, and their evaluations using the root equations have signed heights +C/z^r and -C/z^r, with +C/z^r at the right endpoint and zero at the left. There are no other contacts in y. On the circle the first two interior y levels correspond to symmetric pairs of frequencies. A competitor with no larger norm must have differences of signs <=0, >=0, <=0 at the contacts. Dividing the difference by the positive y produces an affine function, so the middle value is a strict convex combination of the other two and all three must vanish. Cosine expansion recovers (5); in particular b>0 and the middle contact is negative. The constrained Fourier-nonnegative minimum exists (closed constraints, and bounded level sets from evaluation at two distinct positive y); uniqueness then implies a strict gap. Independently ran `python audit_checks/independent_replays.py 4`: 16,001-point epigraph LP and off-grid stationary point checks at orders 0.5, 1, 5, 6 and 12. At order 5 the mesh gave about 0.733730431 with off-grid ripple error about 3.2e-8 and the claimed taps to about 1e-9. The mesh is not the proof; the exact argument covers all real positive orders. Submitted code was inspected, not executed.

value.rationale: Five taps are the first two-free-coefficient case of the same normalized smoother problem; the fifth difference illustrates a natural previous gap. The scalar equations turn qualitative equioscillation into the actual sharp finite-order value and a unique filter, rather than just a numerical or asymptotic prediction. The negative middle contact rigorously explains why Fourier positivity raises the optimum. No utility for larger radius or nonsymmetric filters is assumed.
